Using an RESP for education: separate contribution refunds, EAPs and the net budget

Four graphics connect two available RESP payment sources with outside funding, an illustrative tax allowance and education costs.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

The central idea

The gross RESP withdrawal and the money available for education can differ. Keep contribution refunds, educational assistance payments and the student’s wider tax calculation separate.

01

Identify the payment type before calling it income

The CRA distinguishes contribution refunds from educational assistance payments, or EAPs. Contribution refunds are paid tax-free under the applicable plan conditions. EAPs include grants, bonds and earnings, and are included in the beneficiary student’s income.

This example assumes a Canadian-resident beneficiary remains eligible in a qualifying full-time program beyond the first thirteen consecutive weeks. The promoter is assumed to have confirmed both the contribution amount and gross EAP amount available for the modeled budget after the applicable checks.

The entered EAP capacity is not a calculation from an account’s headline value. It does not independently allocate grants and earnings, verify a beneficiary’s grant history or approve an expense. The source-use chart deliberately shows only the amounts assumed available for this scenario.

02

Confirm capacity before choosing a withdrawal mix

For a qualifying program, the ordinary EAP limit is CAD 8,000 during the first thirteen consecutive weeks. Different period limits apply to specified part-time programs. The model does not calculate those periods or approve an exception; its assumed eligible full-time case is beyond the initial period.

The CRA’s EAP bulletin also describes an administrative review threshold of CAD 29,459 for 2026. That threshold is a promoter guideline, not an unconditional annual withdrawal entitlement. Reasonableness and other eligibility requirements still matter.

The illustration calculates neither grant repayments nor the consequences of a beneficiary becoming ineligible. Those cases require their own review. Confirming payment types and available amounts with the promoter comes before relying on this budget arithmetic.

03

Connect gross EAP, an allowance and contribution cash

The default education budget is CAD 24,000, with CAD 4,000 of confirmed outside funding. The remaining net amount to fund is CAD 20,000. The example has CAD 20,000 of available contributions and CAD 15,000 of confirmed gross EAP capacity.

The selected gross EAP request is CAD 10,000. With a hypothetical 10% tax budget allowance, CAD 1,000 is set aside and CAD 9,000 remains for the education budget. A contribution withdrawal of CAD 11,000 then fills the remaining net need, leaving no funding gap under these assumptions.

Afterward, the model shows CAD 9,000 of contribution capacity and CAD 5,000 of EAP capacity unused. Those are scenario remainders, rather than a guarantee that the same amount will qualify for a later withdrawal. No return or future enrolment schedule is modeled.

04

Keep the budget allowance separate from actual student tax

The allowance percentage is a planning assumption applied only to the modeled EAP. It does not calculate withholding, tuition credits, final tax, benefit changes or the effect of other income. A zero allowance would be an assumption in the tool, not a determination that a student owes no tax.

The model caps the gross EAP at the request, confirmed capacity and the remaining education budget after outside funding, before that allowance. The last cap is a voluntary cash-budget convention. It is not an additional legal EAP limit or a method for determining a promoter’s approval.

Contribution cash fills any remaining need only up to its entered availability. If those two sources and outside funding are insufficient, the waterfall ends negative and the funding-gap metric is positive. Outside funding above the full budget can instead leave unassigned cash.

05

Compare the sources left after funding the same budget

The request curves hold the budget and available sources fixed while varying the gross EAP request. They show how the remaining contribution amount and unused EAP capacity change. The curves do not optimize tax across several study years or recommend one mix.

The matrix changes education costs and confirmed outside funding. Each cell calculates the extra amount needed after the selected withdrawal assumptions. Its cost levels are hypothetical, rather than tuition statistics or a statement of expenses an RESP promoter will accept.

A practical review needs actual eligible costs, proof of enrolment, confirmed payment capacity and a separate tax estimate. The four graphics connect those inputs to a net funding ledger while keeping the RESP’s payment rules and the household’s spending decision distinct.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Charts labelled “Official statistics” or “Derived from official statistics” identify their source periods. Other charts are hypothetical scenarios. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. CRA · Payments from an RESP ↗

    Contribution refunds, EAP composition, beneficiary income and initial-period rules; reviewed 25 October 2026. No personal withdrawal entitlement is determined.

  2. CRA · RESP Bulletin No. 1R3 ↗

    Promoter reasonableness review, records and 2026 administrative EAP threshold. The model assumes applicable plan, grant, beneficiary and expense checks are already satisfied.

  3. Government of Canada · Pay for education using the RESP ↗

    Promoter requests, enrolment evidence and the distinction between education-payment sources. All budget amounts and the allowance percentage are hypothetical.
